passage:
The ferry at Wicken Staithe is a flat boat on a chain, and for one summer I was the person who turned the wheel. The crossing is ninety yards. It takes four minutes in still water and rather longer when the wind comes down the reach, and in either case it is too short for a conversation and too long for silence. I was seventeen. I had the job because my aunt kept the shop on the north bank and had said something to somebody.

In the drawer of the wheelhouse there was a notebook left by the man who had the ferry before me, and the last page he had used was still open. Date, hour, name, and nothing else: the entries were plain. Nobody had asked me to continue it. I continued it because the page was open, and because writing gave me something to do with my hands while people came aboard, which is a thing you want when you are seventeen and must stand four minutes from a stranger.

By the middle of July the book had a rhythm. Mr Ayre crossed at ten past seven and again at six. The Vane girls crossed on Thursdays with a basket carried between them. A man whose name I never learned crossed once a fortnight with a fishing rod he never used, and for him I wrote rod, again. I was not making a study of anybody. I was avoiding the four minutes.

At the end of August a woman called Mrs Tolley asked whether she might look at the book. She turned back to the second week of June, found the line with her own name on it, and said, without needing to read it twice, that was the day I went to see my sister. Then she said, we all wondered what you were putting down about us. It had not occurred to me, in eleven weeks, that the book was being read as anything but what it was to me.

I have thought about it since and I can get no further than the fact of it. I was not watching them; they believed I was, and crossed anyway, and some of them — I know this now — took a little care over how they came aboard. The book is in my aunt's house still. It records ninety yards of water, a hundred and forty days, and not one thing I meant it to.
prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with
choices: a record kept to avoid talking to passengers, and the discovery that the passengers had read it as attention to them
a record kept out of duty to a predecessor, and the discovery that it had become the only history of the crossing
a record kept as a study of a village's habits, and the discovery that its subjects had begun to perform for it
a record kept to pass a slow summer, and the discovery that its writer remembered the season only through it
correct_answer: a record kept to avoid talking to passengers, and the discovery that the passengers had read it as attention to them
explanation: The second paragraph gives the motive — writing "gave me something to do with my hands while people came aboard" — and the third repeats it flatly: "I was avoiding the four minutes." The fourth paragraph supplies the discovery, in Mrs Tolley's "we all wondered what you were putting down about us," and the fifth turns it over. The duty reading is refused in the same breath the notebook is introduced: "Nobody had asked me to continue it." The study reading is refused by "I was not making a study of anybody," which leaves the performing-subjects clause resting on nothing the passage asserts about the writer's purpose. The remembering reading takes the last paragraph's inventory — "ninety yards of water, a hundred and forty days" — as the point of the passage, but that sentence ends by saying the book records "not one thing I meant it to."

passage:
When Harbridge set about marking the six hundredth year of its market charter, the committee's first job looked like the easiest on the list: to fix the date on which market day had moved from Tuesday to Saturday, so that the anniversary supper could be held on the right night of the week.

Two records survive. The parish ledger, kept by successive vicars in one continuous hand until 1881, notes under the heading Michaelmas 1874 that the market is henceforth held upon the Saturday. The account book of Josiah Lound, a carrier who brought goods up from the coast and billed by the trip, shows Tuesday deliveries to the market stalls through the whole of 1875, and his first Saturday delivery in April 1876. Both books are plainly genuine, and neither keeper had any reason to be careless about the day of the week: one was writing for his successors, the other for people who paid him.

The committee's researcher was a retired schoolmistress named Dorcas Whate, and she gave four months to it. She found a third source and it did not help. A newspaper of 1877 congratulated the town upon its Saturday market, now these several years established, which sits as comfortably with 1874 as with 1876.

She also found that a leaf had been cut from the parish ledger between the entries for 1875 and 1876. The cut is old and the knife was sharp, and there is no way now to learn what was on it. A parish ledger holds burials, charity payments, disputes about pews and the repair of a roof, and a page cut from such a ledger might have been cut for any of them.

The committee met twice more. One faction held that the vicar's entry should govern, since it is the town's own record of its own decision; the other held that a carrier who billed by the trip could not have been wrong for fifteen months about which day he drove. The supper was held on a Saturday in June, and the invitation card, at Whate's suggestion, gave the date of the move as 1874 or 1876. She said afterwards that she had expected to mind the double date more than she did, and that what she minded instead was the leaf.
prompt: According to the second paragraph, Josiah Lound's account book shows

Saturday deliveries from Michaelmas 1874 onwards, with no Tuesday trips after that
no deliveries at all to the market stalls between 1874 and the spring of 1876
Tuesday and Saturday deliveries in the same weeks of 1875 and 1876
correct_answer: Tuesday deliveries through 1875 and a first Saturday delivery in April 1876
explanation: The paragraph gives the carrier's book as "Tuesday deliveries to the market stalls through the whole of 1875, and his first Saturday delivery in April 1876." The Michaelmas 1874 date belongs to the other record, the parish ledger, and is what the carrier's book is being set against. A gap in deliveries and a period of both days together are shapes the evidence would have to take for the two records to agree, and neither is on the page.

Reeda Salt has split willow in the same shed at Ninnis Cove for fifty-one years. A rod of willow is split down its length into skeins, and the makers of that valley split into three. Reeda splits into four. A four-way skein is narrower and takes longer to prepare, and a basket woven from four-way skeins holds its shape at the rim in a way that a visitor can see by pressing it with a thumb.

The shop was close, he adds, and in August the door stood open all day.

Neither account can now be tested. The bed behind the chapel was built over in 1979, when the surgery was extended, and the low shop came down the same decade. Ilse Fenwick has been warden of the shingle bar at Skerry Ord for twelve seasons, and for twelve seasons she has counted the nests of the terns that breed on it. The count is her own: nobody else has made one there, before her or beside her.

In her sixth season a storm in early May took the top off the bar and put shingle over the landward half of the colony. She expected the count to fall, and wrote in the log that she expected it. It rose in each of the two seasons that followed, and has stayed up through a run of four mild springs since.

Three things could account for the rise and she cannot separate them. A bar eight miles to the south lost most of its shingle in the same storm, and its birds went somewhere. In her fifth season she had begun walking the bar in two passes instead of one, having found that a single pass missed nests under the weed line. Also in her fifth season the wardens fenced the landward edge with chestnut paling, which keeps dogs off the upper shingle. All three begin within a year of one another, and no season in her record contains one of them without the others.

The county asks its wardens each autumn for one sentence on the season for the annual report. Fenwick sent five. The first said that the colony had grown by about a third since her sixth season. The other four said what the first could not be taken to mean: that a count made one way for four years and another way for eight is two counts; that the southern bar has not been surveyed; and that she would not name a cause. The report printed the first sentence and stopped.

She keeps her own copy of the paragraph in the log, under the entry for the year it describes. She has said that she does not blame the county, which asked for a sentence and was sent five, and that she would send five again.

In 1892 a schoolteacher named Agnes Loom travelled to the northern Italian lakes and kept a diary of ninety pages. It came to a small press in 2003 through her great-niece, and the press gave it to a local historian, Merrick Sale, to edit.

Sale found that six of the ninety pages are taken, nearly word for word, from one of the guidebooks sold at the stations in those years. The six cover the week at Como. They are in the same hand as the rest of the diary and in the same ink, so they were not pasted in or copied out by somebody else; Loom wrote them herself, from the book.

He has described the three courses open to him. He could cut the six pages, and lose the week at Como altogether. He could print them without remark, and let a reader take for Loom's what is not hers. Or he could say so, and say it in a place and a manner of his choosing, which is where the difficulty actually lay.

What he did was to set the six pages in a smaller type, with no note beside them, and an explanation at the back of the volume. A reviewer in a county journal objected that the smaller type passes a judgement Sale had declined to write down, and that a reader who never turns to the back is left to guess at what the type means. Sale answered that he had wanted a reader to meet those pages as Loom's first readers met them, and to be able to learn their source afterwards.

No copy of the guidebook has been found among Loom's things, and her letters of that summer do not mention buying one. The borrowing is known from the wording of the pages and from nothing else.
